report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: CortexLens: Systematically Decoding Interpretable Visual Patterns from Human Visual Cortex

text.text: Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information remains a fundamental challenge in cognitive neuroscience.
Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently been applied to fMRI to discover visual features represented in the visual cortex.

Existing approaches, however, depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery, and report limited discovery of the low-level visual features processed in early retinotopic visual regions that play an essential role in human visual cognition.
We propose an automatic framework that systematically discovers visual features encoded in the human visual cortex, encompassing both high-level and low-level visual features.

The framework decomposes fMRI responses across the full visual hierarchy with Matryoshka sparse autoencoders applied per region of interest, interprets the resulting fMRI activity patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to recover the low-level visual features that language-based interpretation fails to capture.

On the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and on the Brain Encoder Generated Dataset (BEGD), a separate set of synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder, the low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable low-level visual features from early retinotopic visual regions, where prior language-based pipelines report limited discovery.
The high-level stream recovers interpretable semantic visual features on both datasets and generalizes to BOLD5000.

Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation: fMRI activity patterns whose true representation is a low-level visual feature can be misidentified as a semantic visual feature when that feature co-varies with a salient semantic visual feature.
Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information is a central question in cognitive neuroscience.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) offers a non-invasive view of cortical activity during perception, and large-scale datasets now let us study natural-image representations across the visual hierarchy (Allen et al., 2022; Gifford et al., 2023).

Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently emerged as a promising route for interpretability.

text.text: These advances, however, leave two gaps.

First, in coverage: in the literature, existing methods recover far fewer patterns in early retinotopic visual regions than in higher cortex, explaining far fewer candidate concepts in V1, V2, and V3 compared to regions such as the extrastriate body area (EBA) (Wasserman et al., 2025).

text.text: The concepts assigned to early retinotopic visual regions are also implausible: V1 and V2 patterns are labeled clock tower, clear sky, and clock, and a V3 pattern top left, a retinotopic coordinate rather than a visual concept.

Second, in methodology: the prevailing recipe prompts a vision-language model (VLM) openendedly on a latent's top-activating images and treats the resulting explanation as its meaning, conflating feature recovery (identifying what a latent responds to) with explanation (naming it).
Recovery thus becomes contingent on interpretability-a feature must be nameable by an agent to be found at all (Table 1).

text.text: We therefore hypothesize that low-level visual features are recovered less often than semantic features and are more often mischaracterized by open-ended language-based interpretation.
In this work, we propose a pipeline that systematically and automatically decodes both high-level and lowlevel visual features represented in visual cortex.

The pipeline decomposes fMRI responses with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), interprets the resulting patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to detect the low-level visual patterns that purely language-based interpretation tends to miss.

We instantiate this framework on the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) (Allen et al., 2022), augmented with synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder (Adeli et al., 2026) applied to the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset, decomposing each region of interest with a Matryoshka SAE (Bussmann et al., 2025).

text.text: The resulting dictionary spans 8 subjects and 20 regions across the full visual hierarchy.

Using these feature channels, we recover thousands of interpretable low-level visual patterns in early retinotopic visual regions that prior pipelines fail to recover, with interpretability comparable to semantic features.
Features are recovered and validated through statistical tests in both streams to reduce the dependency on agents.
We additionally replicate the high-level stream on BOLD5000 (Chang et al., 2019) in 3 subjects and 4 regions (LOC, OPA, PPA, RSC), yielding 2,933 semantic visual features across 1,202 units.

text.text: Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation and shows that interpretability and feature recovery are distinct objectives.
We summarize our contributions: • A unified fMRI pattern decoding framework.

We present an SDL-based interpretability framework that recovers high-level and low-level visual patterns in a unified pipeline, achieving substantial gains on early retinotopic visual regions where prior methods fail.
• Large-scale interpretable pattern dictionary.
We construct a large dictionary of identified visual patterns, with natural-language interpretations and quantitative quality metrics, to support follow-up neuroscience and interpretability research.
• A warning for mechanistic interpretability.

We show that many patterns, especially those encoding low-level visual structure, can be systematically misinterpreted by VLM-based pipelines, revealing a failure mode that mechanistic interpretability must guard against.
• A dissociation between recovery and explanation.
We show empirically that how selectively a unit encodes a feature carries little information about how well that feature can be explained, and that the dissociation is bi-directional.

First, to provide a detailed representation of the semantic concepts every image carries, we prompt a VLM (Gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview) to convert each image into a structured caption covering its primary focus, salient objects, setting, colors, activity, and any visible text (Appendix B.3).
These captions are then atomized into standalone semantic visual features, and deduplicated into a canonical dictionary of the semantic visual features in the stimuli.
For each image, we shortlist features from that dictionary by lexical match and high CLIP cosine similarity between each dictionary feature and the image's caption.
Finally, we use Gemini-3.1-flash-lite to verify whether each shortlisted visual feature is supported by the image's caption and structured fields (Appendix B.4).

Second, to recover the semantic features of each unit, we separately retrieve all semantic visual features that are systematically enriched or depleted in its top-activating images, beyond or below their natural prevalence, as detailed in Algorithm 2.
To test whether selectivity extends past the images used to recover the feature, we additionally repeat the enrichment check on activation ranks 81-100.

Third, we interpret each unit with at least one recovered feature under a two-stage procedure described in Section 3.5, by passing all its recovered features to the explainer as text, together with the montage of its top-20 activating images.
We use a different schema for units with only enriched features versus those carrying at least one depleted feature (prompts in Appendix B.5 and B.6).
We use the following metrics to evaluate the units we identify from our SDL pipelines.
Enrichment.

Enrichment is the fold-change of a recovered feature's prevalence within a unit's top-N top sample over its global base rate, with significance from a Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected hypergeometric test: where p(f) u is the feature's prevalence in the unit's top-N top sample and p(f) its global base rate.
For HVF, hypergeometric p-values were Benjamini-Hochberg corrected separately within each unit and activation-rank window across the full 3,006-feature dictionary.
For LVF, the 15,284 unit-by-channel hypergeometric p-values were corrected jointly across the study.
Recall-type metrics are omitted as structurally uninformative in a 20-image sample.
We also test whether units with retained features contribute more to reconstruction than units without them with intervention tests, apart from feature recovery (Appendix H).
AUROC.
AUROC is the area under the ROC curve for LVF features, with top-N top membership as the binary target and the expression score (ES) as the continuous score: where S u is the unit's top-N top sample.

AIS is computed by a two-stage explainer-evaluator protocol, in which one VLM interprets a unit's top-N top sample and a second, independent VLM judges each image against the resulting explanation: where e u is the explainer's explanation for unit u, x j are the unit's top-N top samples, and N top = 20.
The name apparent marks that this is the second model's score on that sample and is to be distinguished from human interpretability.
The explainer is GPT-5.4-mini, and the evaluator is Gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview.

Finally, intervention tests show that units with recovered features contribute more to reconstruction than units without them (mean ∆r 2.0 × 10 -4 versus 0.61 × 10 -4 ; 110 of 158 subject-ROI cells; Appendix H).
Every recovered primary feature is validated for signal saliency, biological predictability, and enrichment, and retained units are near-monosemantic (1.04 features per unit).
Recovery is robust to stricter thresholds-70.3% of features hold at q ≤ 0.01 and 49.7% at q ≤ 0.001-and in effect size, with 53.0% reaching 3× base-rate enrichment and 17.7% reaching 5×.

Among the factors of the dataset, ROI, subject, and channel, selectivity is dominated by channel identity (partial η² = 0.468, model R² = 0.569), while recovery counts are co-driven by ROI and channel (Poisson pseudo-R² = 0.393).

Recovery is stable across ROIs except hV4 (5.3% of features) but uneven across channels, from relative depth (28.8%) to opponent color (7.2%); quantity and selectivity trade off inversely across channels, a pattern we trace to feature sparsity in Section 4.3.

Recovered features are mostly interpretable, with a median AIS of 0.700 (65.7% ≥ 0.5, 47.3% ≥ 0.8); interpretability is dominated by channel identity (partial η² = 0.099, F = 125.4, p = 4.91 × 10 -151 ), with median AIS highest for symmetry and oriented energy and lowest for skeleton.
Notably, the most selective channel (skeleton) is the least interpretable, a dissociation we return to in Section 5.1.

The selectivity of recovered LVF features is largely explained by their natural sparsity.
We measured selectivity by AUROC (top-20 activation membership as target, expression score as continuous score), which-unlike enrichment-does not share the prevalence factor with sparsity.
Recovered features are generally selective, ranging from relative depth (median AUROC 0.704) to skeleton (0.929), and channel identity again dominates (R² = 0.380, partial η² = 0.255).

text.text: We therefore suggest that a feature is selectively recovered when the architectural sparsity of the SAE aligns with the natural sparsity of the feature it encodes; when a feature is far denser than the sparsity constraint, the unit capturing it tends to subset the images containing it under impaired selectivity.
We tested this by removing the TopK constraint from the Matryoshka encoder, leaving the linear map followed by JumpReLU, and retraining on NSD alone.
Where a feature is as rare as that constraint, or rarer, mean AUROC is already high, and removing TopK lowers it: skeleton moves from 0.917 to 0.865.
Where a feature is present in more images than the constraint keeps active, mean AUROC rises: relative depth moves from 0.600 to 0.707.
The with-TopK means pool both NSD replications and the without-TopK means are rep1 only.

Our experiments show that selectivity and interpretability are largely independent across recovered primary features on NSD and BEGD (Spearman ρ = -0.084 between AUROC and AIS).
Many features are selectively encoded but difficult to explain, while others are readily described despite weak selectivity.
This contrast is especially clear across channels: skeleton features are the most selective yet least interpretable, whereas relative depth shows the opposite trend.

A similar lack of correlation appears in the HVF stream between a unit's strongest enrichment and its AIS, although the two streams evaluate different objects and need not share the same underlying mechanism.
We believe this distinction reveals some fundamental limitations for prevalent feature discovery pipelines used in mechanistic interpretability.
If a feature is retained only when an agent can describe it convincingly, selective but poorly verbalized features will be systematically missed.
The two ns pairs are symmetry and opponent color; each has only two or three features on the smaller side.
Our results also demonstrate that language-based explanations can identify the wrong feature.

Since early retinotopic visual regions are primarily associated with visual properties such as orientation, spatial frequency, and position (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962; Kay et al., 2008) rather than semantic visual features (Kanwisher et al., 1997), semantic visual representations are less expected based on our prior knowledge.

text.text: When a low-level representation is interpreted through a semantic proxy, however, the explainer may still identify a semantic exemplar that co-occurs with the underlying feature rather than the feature itself, merely due to its agentic biases-a failure mode we term masquerade.
We quantitatively demonstrate this by the most frequent semantic concept we have discovered from these areas-sky.
Sky was recovered in 6,744 of the 12,308 units (54.8%), against 2,386 units for the next most frequent feature, outdoor natural scene (19.4%).
Sky was recovered at a median enrichment of 7.24 times over base rate and reached a median AIS of 0.65.
Nonetheless, the explanatory power of sky was systematically weaker when compared with the low-level visual features recovered from the same units.
We first identified 388 units from which sky was semantically recovered, and at least one low-level visual feature was also recovered under the LVF stream (411 low-level features in total).
We then compared their presence in the images that evoke the unit across these 411 pairs.

In the median case, two-thirds of the sky-absent images among a unit's top-20 activating images still express its low-level visual feature (0.667), and the low-level visual feature is present in more of the top-activating sample than sky is (0.800 against 0.650).
The semantic feature therefore accounts for less of a unit's topactivating sample than the low-level visual feature recovered from the same unit.

text.text: No prior study is a direct numerical baseline for CortexLens.

An eligible study would decompose visually evoked fMRI without supervision, discover within-ROI activity patterns, and automatically identify and evaluate the visual features those patterns represent.

Among the methods in Table 1, only Brain-Explore (Wasserman et al., 2025) meets the task criteria, and its numbers are not comparable: it uses pattern-hypothesis alignment for discovery and for interpretability, whereas CortexLens separates statistically tested recovery from explanation quality.

text.text: The public release did not include the pipeline, concept dictionary, and ranking data a common-protocol reanalysis would need.
A direct comparison will require the same dataset, feature ontology, activation sample, and evaluation protocol.

CortexLens learns fMRI activity patterns across the human visual hierarchy through sparse decomposition, and recovers and interprets the semantic visual features and low-level visual features in the images that evoke those patterns through an automatic pipeline.

On NSD and BEGD this yields thousands of interpretable low-level visual features in early retinotopic visual regions, where existing approaches depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery and report limited discovery there.
Across NSD, BEGD, and BOLD5000, CortexLens also discovered a rich collection of interpretable semantic visual features represented by the fMRI activity patterns across the visual cortex.
Together, we believe CortexLens provides a comprehensive framework for studying visual representations in the visual cortex.

(Step 2) Each unit's encoded visual features are recovered in two parallel streams under a shared structure.

Each recovered feature passes the gates stated for its stream.
(Step 3) Both streams share enrichment as a recovery metric; AUROC is additionally computed for the LVF stream.
Features are then explained in natural language and assessed by an apparent interpretability score (AIS).
